questions.title: Why does GRPO’s token‑level importance ratio lead to instability when responses become long?
questions.question_body: GRPO uses the ratio $w_{i,t}(	heta)= rac{	heta(y_{i,t} ig|x,y_{i,<t})}{	heta_{	ext{old}}(y_{i,t} ig|x,y_{i,<t})}$ at each token. In the paper it is claimed that this “fails to perform the intended distribution‑correction role” and hence causes high‑variance noise that accumulates over long sequences. How exactly does applying a single‑token importance weight remain a valid importance sampling correction if we only have one sample from that token distribution? Is there a simple example (e.g., a two‑token sequence) that illustrates why this weight does not correct for the off‑policy distribution and why it can cause exploding gradients when clipped?

questions.title: What is the theoretical justification for normalizing the sequence‑level importance ratio by sequence length in GSPO?
questions.question_body: $s_i(	heta)= ig( rac{	heta(y_i|x)}{	heta_{	ext{old}}(y_i|x)} ig)^{1/|y_i|}$ is introduced to reduce variance. The paper says varying length would otherwise require different clipping ranges. Can someone explain why the $1/|y_i|$ exponent equalizes the scale across lengths? What would happen to $s_i(	heta)$ if we omitted this normalization – would it still be bounded, and how would that affect clipping stability?

questions.title: How does GSPO’s gradient derivation avoid assigning different weights to tokens inside the same sequence?
questions.question_body:
In Equation (10) the gradient contains $ rac{1}{|y_i|}
abla_	heta  igl[	heta(y_{i,t} ig|x,y_{i,<t}) igr]$, while in GRPO (Equation 11) each token gets multiplied by its own importance ratio $w_{i,t}(	heta)$. Since $w_{i,t}(	heta)$ can vary widely within a sequence, why does GSPO not suffer from the same variance? Is the absence of token‑level weighting enough to guarantee more stable learning, or is there another subtle factor?

questions.title: Can you clarify why GSPO eliminates the need for Routing Replay in MoE training?
questions.question_body: Routing Replay was introduced to keep expert activations stable so that $w_{i,t}(	heta)$ could be computed reliably for each token. GSPO supposedly sidesteps this by using only $s_i(	heta) =  igl(	frac{	heta(y_i)}{	heta_{	ext{old}}(y_i)} igr)^{1/|y_i|}$, which is claimed to be insensitive to per‑token expert changes. Why exactly does a change in expert activation for one token not affect the overall likelihood enough to destabilize $s_i(	heta)$? Are there empirical evidences or theoretical bounds that explain how much variance remains when experts shift?

questions.title: Why are the clipping ranges in GSPO two orders of magnitude smaller than those in GRPO?
questions.question_body: In §4.1 GSPO uses clipping ranges like $[3	imes10^{-4}, 4	imes10^{-4}]$ whereas GRPO uses [0.2, 0.27]. The paper notes that these numbers are chosen after careful tuning but does not explain why such a drastic difference is necessary. Could someone elaborate on what property of $s_i(	heta)$ (vs. $w_{i,t}(	heta)$) dictates that we must use much tighter clipping? Does this relate to the variance reduction from length normalization or something else?

questions.title: How do we compute and interpret 'mean' and 'std' of rewards within a group in GRPO/GSPO?
questions.question_body: $	ilde A_i =  rac{r(x,y_i)-	ext{mean} igl(brace r(x,y_j) igr) igr)}{	ext{std} igl(brace r(x,y_j) igr)}$. In practice, with large batch sizes and diverse queries – especially when many sequences are short – how stable are these statistics? Could inaccurate estimates of mean/std cause bias or high variance in the advantage? Also, why use standardisation instead of raw rewards or reward differences?

questions.title: `GSPO-token` appears identical to `GSPO` when all token advantages are equal – is there any real difference?
questions.question_body:
`GSPO-token` uses a per‑token advantage $	ilde A_{i,t}$ but keeps $s_{i,t}(	heta)$ numerically equal to $s_i(	heta)`. When $	ilde A_{i,t}$ differs across tokens, equation (12) shows an unbalanced weighting of $
abla_	heta$ terms. How does this finer granular adjustment affect learning dynamics compared to plain GSPO? Are there scenarios (e.g., multi‑turn dialogue) where per‑token advantages provide a clear performance benefit?

questions.title: What assumptions underlie the claim that GSPO’s sequence‐level objective is ‘well‑posed’ compared to GRPO’s?
questions.question_body: "Ill‐posed" in §3 refers to misapplication of importance sampling and accumulation of noise over long sequences. Could someone formalise what makes an RL objective well‑posed here? Specifically, is it about unbiasedness, bounded variance, or some other property? How do we verify that GSPO satisfies those criteria while GRPO does not?

questions.title: $s_{i,t}(	heta)$ as defined in Eq.(12) contains an `sg` operation – what exactly is its purpose?
questions.question_body:
`sg` denotes stop‐gradient; thus $ rac{	heta(y_{i,t} ig|x,y_{i,<t})}{sg[	heta(y_{i,t} ig|x,y_{i,<t})]}$ evaluates numerically to 1 but contributes no gradient flow. Why do we need this sacrifice of gradient for implementation purposes? Does it simply prevent double counting of gradients from $
abla_	heta s_i$, or does it serve another role?

questions.title: "Reward” is defined as being bounded between 0 and 1 – how critical is this range for Algorithm design?
questions.question_body: "The verifier returns reward r(x,y)	imesin[0,1]"; yet we only see standardisation later using mean and std over group rewards. Would a different reward scaling (e.g., raw log probabilities or negative loss values) break any part of the derivations? Are there pros/cons regarding clipping when rewards are not normalized?
